transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Anderson, thank you for coming in. I need to discuss your treatment from yesterday with you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Of course. Dr. Miller mentioned there might be some adjustments to my cycle, but he didn't go into detail.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am so sorry. I made a serious mistake in calculating your chemotherapy dose yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I used your weight from your initial admission three months ago instead of your current weight. Because you've lost a significant amount of weight during this treatment, you received a dose that was too high for your current body mass.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I was told by the nursing staff that the dose was standard for my stage. Now you're saying it was wrong?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was. I am personally responsible for this error. I failed to verify your most recent weight before the order was sent, and for that, I sincerely apologize.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is very concerning. I've spent my entire career in hospital administration. I know exactly how these checks are supposed to happen. How did this even get past the pharmacy?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You're right that there are checks in place. However, the accountability for the initial calculation lies with me, and I let you down. I am not making excuses for why it happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel incredibly vulnerable right now. I'm already struggling with the side effects of the regular dose, and now I've had an overdose?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is a lot to take in.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's more than a lot. I'm wondering if I've caused permanent damage to my organs or if I'm going to have a much more severe reaction than—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have to move through this quickly because I have a clinic starting in ten minutes, but we need to focus on the monitoring.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm sorry, you're rushing me? I just told you I'm terrified about the toxicity of the drug and you're checking your watch?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I just want to make sure we get to the solution.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The solution doesn't matter if I don't understand the risk. Dr. Miller said the regimen was precise. Now you're telling me there was an "issue." What exactly did I receive?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There was a discrepancy in the dosing parameters. Things didn't go quite right with the weight update.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is not an answer. Did I receive a toxic dose? Give me a number.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was an overage based on the previous weight.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are being incredibly vague. I want to know the exact milligram difference between what I was supposed to get and what I actually got.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's a bit complex. Let's just say we are monitoring you closely.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am not interested in "monitoring." I am interested in the facts of the error.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand this is frustrating.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Frustrating? It's a medication error in a high-alert drug.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Let's wrap this up so we can look at the plan.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am not finished. I want to know why the information I got from the other clinician contradicts what you're saying now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There was some confusion in the communication chain.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's a systemic excuse. I'm asking why I was told one thing and now another.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I apologize for the confusion.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You've apologized, but you aren't explaining.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Here is how we are going to handle this. First, I have already scheduled a blood chemistry panel for tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM to check your kidney and liver function. Second, I have coordinated with the oncology pharmacist to create a new, corrected dosing sheet that will be double-signed by two attending physicians for every subsequent dose. Third, I want you to keep a detailed log of any new symptoms, specifically nausea or neuropathy, and email that to my secure line every evening this week. Finally, I am filing a formal incident report with the risk management department today to ensure our weight-verification protocol is changed so this cannot happen to another patient.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And if the blood work shows toxicity?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: If the labs show any elevation, we will immediately start a hydration protocol to flush your system. I will call you personally by 11:00 AM tomorrow with those results.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I expect that call. I also expect a written copy of the actual dose administered versus the intended dose for my own records.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will have that printed and in your chart before you leave the building today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I still don't feel like you've actually told me how dangerous this was.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will send you the lab results as soon as they arrive.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('move through this quickly', 'clinic starting in ten minutes', 'wrap this up') and interrupts the patient's emotional expression.

E.justification: While the error was named early, the resident failed to perform any comprehension checks and later used vague hedging ('discrepancy in dosing parameters') when asked for specifics.

A.justification: Resident uses direct apology language, explicitly takes personal responsibility ('I am personally responsible'), and maintains this accountability despite the patient's pushback.

R.justification: Resident provides only generic validation ('I know this is a lot to take in', 'I understand this is frustrating') without naming specific emotions or engaging emotional bids.

T.justification: Resident provides specific next steps with timelines (8:00 AM labs, 11:00 AM call), a named patient role (detailed symptom log), and a prevention plan (incident report/protocol change).
